title: The recall, latency, memory triangle
summary: Recall in ANN means agreement with brute force, and the returns diminish hard: measured on real embeddings, scanning 1.7 percent of the data recovers 54 percent of the right answers and 13 percent recovers 95 percent. Which recall you need is a property of your whole pipeline, not your index.
html:
Yesterday's exact search is correct and does not scale. Every index in Phase 2 buys speed by being wrong sometimes. Today is about the currency that purchase is made in, because you are about to meet six index families and they are all trading the same three things.

Recall, defined properly

Recall here is not the retrieval metric from Day 14. It is narrower and it is measured against yourself:

recall@k = |approximate top-k  AND  exact top-k| / k

Not "did we find the right answer". Did we find what brute force would have found. Exact search is the reference, which is the practical reason Day 15 said you never stop running it. A recall of 0.95 at k=10 means your index returned 9.5 of the 10 vectors a linear scan would have, averaged over queries.

Note what this does not tell you. An index at 0.95 recall might be dropping the tenth-best neighbour every time, which nobody notices, or the best one occasionally, which is a bad day. Same number, different products.

The triangle

Three quantities, and you get to fix two:

  • Recall. How often you agree with brute force.
  • Latency. Time per query, which is mostly how many vectors you looked at (Day 15: it is a bandwidth problem).
  • Memory. Bytes resident, vectors plus whatever the index adds on top.

Want higher recall at fixed memory? Look at more candidates, pay latency. Want lower latency at fixed recall? Spend memory on a structure that finds candidates better. Want both cheap? Compress the vectors and lose recall. Every technique from Day 17 to Day 30 is one of those three moves.

The curve, measured

I built the simplest possible index to show the shape: cluster the vectors with k-means into 64 lists, then at query time only scan the nprobe nearest clusters. That is IVF, and Day 20 does it properly. Sweeping nprobe from 1 to 64 walks the entire tradeoff.

Run on 6,200 real document embeddings (20 Newsgroups through MiniLM, 384 dimensions), with 300 held out queries and recall measured against exact search:

 nprobe  %scanned  recall@10  ms/query  speedup
      1      1.7%      0.543     0.044     2.4x
      2      3.4%      0.734     0.063     1.7x
      4      6.7%      0.879     0.098     1.1x
      8     13.2%      0.951     0.194     0.6x
     16     26.0%      0.983     0.378     0.3x
     32     50.8%      0.998     0.762     0.1x
     64    100.0%      1.000     1.289     0.1x

Read the first two columns and ignore the rest for a moment, because that relationship is the one that transfers:

Looking at 1.7 percent of the data recovers 54 percent of the right answers. Looking at 13 percent recovers 95 percent. Looking at everything recovers everything.

Sharply diminishing returns, and that is the entire economic case for approximate search. The last 5 percent of recall costs more than the first 95 percent. Whether you should buy it depends on what happens downstream, and usually you should not.

The part of my own result that failed

The speedup column is embarrassing. IVF is slower than exact search here at any nprobe above 2, and the reason is Day 15. Six thousand vectors is 9 MB. Brute force is one large matrix multiply that streams perfectly and finishes in 0.108 ms. My IVF does Python-level list concatenation and gathers scattered rows, which destroys locality to save work that was not expensive.

This is the "use a flat index below 100k" guidance showing up in my own measurement, and it is worth more than a clean result would have been. The recall curve is real and transfers to any scale. The latency column is an artifact of benchmarking at a size where the problem does not exist. When you read ANN benchmarks, check the corpus size before believing the speedups.

At a million vectors the same curve reads differently: scanning 13 percent instead of 100 percent turns a 93 ms query into roughly 12 ms, for one missing neighbour in twenty.

The third axis, which the curve above hides

That sweep held memory fixed, so it only shows two corners of the triangle. The third is where the index families genuinely diverge, and the numbers are not close.

The IVF index I just built stores 64 centroids and one list id per vector. On 6,200 vectors of 384 dimensions that is about 123 KB of structure on top of 9.5 MB of vectors, roughly 1.3 percent overhead. Almost free.

A graph index is a different proposition. HNSW stores outgoing edges per node, and at a typical 32 neighbours with 4 byte ids that is 128 bytes of edges against a 1,536 byte vector, before counting the upper layers. Call it 10 percent, and it climbs steeply with the connectivity parameter that controls recall. Tomorrow's lesson is partly about why that is worth paying.

Compression runs the axis the other way. Product quantization (Day 21) replaces a 1,536 byte vector with something like 64 bytes, a 24x reduction, and gives back recall in exchange. Same triangle, opposite direction.

Operating points, not winners

"Which index is best" is not a question with an answer. Each index family traces a curve through the triangle, and you choose a point on it based on a constraint you actually have:

ConstraintWhat you pick
Interactive search, 50 ms budget, RAM availablegraph index, tuned to the recall that fits the budget (Days 17 to 19)
Billion vectors, one machine, RAM scarcecompression plus cell-based search (Days 21 to 26)
Offline batch scoring, no latency limitexact, batched (Day 15)
Recall is contractual, cost is notgenerous candidate set plus a reranker (Day 37)

That last row matters more than it looks. If a cross-encoder is going to re-score your top 100 anyway, losing a couple of true neighbours from position 50 changes nothing, because the reranker was going to reorder them regardless. A system with a reranker can run its index at much lower recall than one that serves index output directly. Your acceptable recall is a property of the whole pipeline, not of the index.

This is how the field reports results, and it is why ann-benchmarks plots queries per second against recall rather than publishing a league table. A curve above and to the right of another curve is better. Curves that cross have no winner, only different right answers at different operating points.

You have the axes now. Tomorrow you meet the structure that dominates in-memory vector search, and the small world graph idea underneath it: HNSW.
exercise:
1. Plot your own curve. Take any set of embeddings you have, cluster them with sklearn.cluster.KMeans into sqrt(N) lists, and sweep nprobe from 1 upward. Measure recall@10 against exact search at each step. You only need the first two columns. The shape you get is the shape you will be negotiating with for the rest of Phase 2.

2. Find your own 95 percent point. From that curve, read off what fraction of the data you have to scan for 95 percent recall. Multiply your Day 15 exact latency by that fraction. That product is roughly what a well tuned index would give you, and it tells you whether Phase 2 is worth your time at your corpus size.

3. Decide what recall you actually need. Write down one sentence: does your system show index output directly to a user, or does something re-score it first? If something re-scores it, you can run at 0.85 recall and nobody will ever know. If it does not, you cannot. That single fact constrains every index decision you are about to make.
